extracted.intended_audience: photographers and photojournalists (especially those who want to be featured on The New York Times' social/Instagram accounts) and social photo editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, captioning, and pitching photography for The New York Times' Instagram accounts (@nytimes and @nytarchives); includes editorial tone, caption strategy, and pitching / discovery practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent breadth of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: We try to represent the breadth of New York Times coverage, so you’ll see food photography, celebrity portraiture and the reportage-style work we’re known for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature work by a wide range of staff photographers and topics rather than a single subject area; aim to show the variety of the newsroom's visual reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature the best of visual news and daily-life moments
rubrics_metrics.description: We strive to take a reflective tone and focus on the best of the visual news and daily life moments caught by our photographers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize images that are strong storytelling pieces or evocative daily-life reportage that stand on their own visually and narratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captions are as important as images
rubrics_metrics.description: We consider our captions just as important as the images: We try to tell full (albeit short) stories on Instagram.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write concise captions that convey a complete New York Times story — include context, stakes, or a short narrative instead of just a label or credits; use captions to complement and deepen the image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the subject's voice when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If we use a picture of a person, we include that person’s voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible incorporate quotes or first-person perspective from the photographed subject to add immediacy and human interest to the caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the story behind the photo (contextual details)
rubrics_metrics.description: We tell the story behind the photo — was the photographer in a helicopter? Did he or she walk for 6 hours to reach the spot pictured?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include production/context details that illuminate how the image was made or the conditions surrounding it when those details strengthen the story; these make captions more engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: conversational but faithful to reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: We try to be conversational, but there are times when we don’t veer far from the reporters’ wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a generally conversational voice on captions for accessibility, but retain accuracy and reporter-provided wording when it better serves the story or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curatorial goals for @nytarchives: surprise, delight, informal background
rubrics_metrics.description: The @nytarchives account is meant to be fun. Our primary focus there is to bring our followers a sense of surprise and delight... we’re writing in a fairly informal tone. We don’t want to teach readers about history or focus on 'this day in history,' but to provide interesting background for eye-catching photos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For archival posts favor an informal, entertaining framing that provides interesting background or anecdotes rather than a didactic historical lesson; prioritize eye-catching imagery and surprising facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching: concise synopsis + multiple images
rubrics_metrics.description: I’d prefer to see a brief synopsis with some additional information attached, and I like to see more than a few images to know if something is working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching, keep text short and attach multiple representative images (not a single photo) so editors can assess consistency and quality; include relevant contextual info but avoid long, wordy pitches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching: preferred channel and professional etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t love being pitched on Facebook Messenger. Email is best — then I can easily share something with other Times editors, if it makes sense. Don’t call a female editor 'sir'!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch via email so pitches can be forwarded internally; use proper salutations and professional tone; avoid informal/messenger platforms and basic etiquette mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photographer discovery: follow bylines and social feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: I pay attention to bylines. I follow a lot of photographers on social media — not only to see their work, but to see what and who they’re sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be discoverable, maintain strong bylines and an active, curated social presence; share both professional and select personal work to showcase voice and networks (but know where to draw the line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Share personal work thoughtfully and disclose affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t mind seeing personal photos, but I think photographers should know where to draw the line. I do think it’s important to share personal work or work you’re doing for other organizations. (Just be sure you’re clear on that organization’s guidelines for social media.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal projects can demonstrate range — include them — but clarify if work was produced for other organizations and follow those organizations' social-media rules; avoid confusing or conflicting presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use captions and profile linking to direct readers to longer coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Visit the link in our profile to read more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an image is tied to a longer article or multimedia package, use captions and profile links/CTAs to send followers to full coverage; captions can include short calls-to-action when appropriate.
